human_facing_meta_review.summary: This paper proposes a knowledge-driven methodology for automatically generating large-scale labeled training data for event extraction by combining Freebase (world knowledge) and FrameNet (linguistic knowledge). The core contribution is a soft distant supervision (SDS) framework adapted from relation extraction to event extraction, featuring: (1) Key Rate (KR) metric combining Role Saliency and Event Relevance for argument prioritization, (2) Trigger Rate (TR) metric combining Trigger Candidate Frequency and Trigger Event Type Frequency for trigger detection, (3) FrameNet-based filtering and expansion for trigger quality improvement, and (4) Multi-instance learning for noise mitigation. The paper generates 72,611 automatically labeled sentences across 21 Freebase event types with reported quality of 88.9% precision for triggers and 85.4% for arguments (manual evaluation on 500 samples). Automatic evaluation demonstrates utility: combining automatically labeled data with human-annotated ACE data (ACE+ED) achieves F1 of 70.5 (trigger+classification) vs. 69.1 baseline. The work addresses a genuine problem (expensive manual annotation, low event-type coverage) and proposes a reasonable solution with practical dataset contribution. However, the paper exhibits significant methodological gaps: absence of statistical significance testing for all improvements, small and potentially unrepresentative manual evaluation sample (0.69% of dataset, no stratification by event type), unvalidated critical assumptions (Freebase-FrameNet mapping quality), and incomplete ablation studies (no FrameNet filtering vs. expansion decomposition, no DMCNN vs. DMCNN-MIL comparison). The novelty is primarily methodological assembly (adapting distant supervision to event extraction) rather than algorithmic innovation (KR and TR are heuristic combinations of existing features). The paper makes meaningful but incremental contributions with substantial practical value, but methodological limitations prevent higher confidence in reported improvements.
strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation: Paper clearly articulates limitations of supervised event extraction (expensive annotation, low coverage in ACE 2005: 60% of types have <100 samples) and motivates automatic data labeling as a solution.

Sound methodological approach: Four-stage pipeline (key argument detection → trigger detection → FrameNet filtering/expansion → SDS labeling) is logically coherent and addresses specific challenges at each stage. Soft distant supervision assumption is reasonable: sentences with all key arguments + trigger word likely express the event.

Comprehensive evaluation strategy: Paper employs multiple complementary evaluation approaches (manual evaluation on 500 samples with inter-annotator agreement, automatic evaluation on ACE test set with three baselines, held-out evaluation, human evaluation of newly discovered instances), providing multi-faceted validation.

Substantial practical dataset contribution: 72,611 automatically labeled sentences across 21 Freebase event types represents 12× scale increase over ACE 2005 (~6,000 sentences). Dataset is released for community use, providing tangible resource contribution.

Demonstrated practical utility: Combining automatically labeled data with human-annotated ACE data (ACE+ED) improves event extraction performance (F1: 70.5 trigger+classification vs. 69.1 baseline), showing automatically labeled data can augment human-annotated data.
Ablation studies for proposed metrics: Tables 5-6 include ablation studies comparing KR vs. RS/ER and TR vs. TCF/TETF, demonstrating that proposed metrics outperform single-factor baselines.
Clear presentation: Paper is well-written with effective visual aids (Figure 3 contrasting events vs. relations, Table 2 showing concrete examples, Figure 4 architecture overview).
limitations: Absence of statistical significance testing for all reported improvements: No p-values, confidence intervals, or significance tests provided for any improvements in Tables 4-6. Improvements range from 0.2-5.2 F1 points, but without statistical validation, it is unclear whether differences are meaningful or within noise margins. This is a critical methodological flaw that undermines confidence in all quantitative claims.

Manual evaluation sample size and representativeness concerns: Only 500 samples manually evaluated from 72,611 total (0.69% sample rate). No stratification by event type reported; sample may be biased toward high-quality event types. Event type distribution in sample unknown. Inter-annotator agreement of 87.5% indicates 12.5% disagreement; voting mechanism may mask systematic biases. Reported precision figures (88.9%, 85.4%) lack confidence intervals and may overestimate true dataset quality.

Unvalidated critical assumption about Freebase-FrameNet mapping: Equation 7 uses word embedding similarity to map Freebase events to FrameNet frames, but no validation of mapping quality, error analysis, or comparison with alternative mapping methods provided. This is a critical assumption (A4) that directly impacts trigger filtering/expansion effectiveness but remains completely unvalidated.

Incomplete ablation studies: (1) FrameNet filtering vs. expansion effects not decomposed; Table 6 shows combined effect (1.0-1.7 F1 improvement) but unclear which operation drives improvement or whether they have complementary or opposing effects. (2) No direct DMCNN vs. DMCNN-MIL comparison; Section 5.5 claims MIL effectiveness but provides no ablation study. Figures 7-8 lack numerical values; Table 7 incomplete.

Limited generalization scope: Only 4 Freebase event types mapped to ACE for automatic evaluation; generalization to unmapped types unclear. Only 21 of 1,885 Freebase CVTs evaluated; selection criteria not specified. Generalization to all Freebase CVTs or to other knowledge bases (Wikidata, DBpedia) unclear.
open_questions: Are the reported improvements statistically significant? What are the 95% confidence intervals for F1 scores in Tables 4-6? Conduct paired t-tests or bootstrap confidence intervals to determine whether improvements (0.2-5.2 F1 points) are meaningful or within noise margins. This is essential for validating all quantitative claims.

How representative is the 500-sample manual evaluation? What is the distribution of samples across the 21 event types? Does precision vary significantly across event types? Conduct stratified sampling and report precision separately for each event type to assess representativeness and identify potential biases.

What is the quality of Freebase-FrameNet mappings? Manually evaluate a sample of mappings (50-100) to assess accuracy. What is the mapping error rate? How do incorrect mappings impact trigger detection and overall performance? Compare word embedding similarity with alternative mapping methods.

What are the individual contributions of FrameNet filtering vs. expansion? Provide ablation results for: (1) filtering-only (remove noisy verbs), (2) expansion-only (add nominal triggers), (3) both. This will clarify which operation drives the 1.0-1.7 F1 improvement and whether they have complementary or opposing effects.

How much does multi-instance learning contribute to noise mitigation? Provide direct comparison of DMCNN with and without MIL on automatically labeled data. Report precision, recall, F1 for both variants. Provide numerical values for Figures 7-8 (P-R curves). Complete Table 7 with specific precision values and n values.

How do results generalize to unmapped event types and to all 1,885 Freebase CVTs? Explicitly list the 4 event types mapped from Freebase to ACE. Analyze whether improvements are consistent across these 4 types or vary significantly. Discuss why only 4 types could be mapped and whether this limits generalizability. Evaluate on additional event types if possible.

What types of errors occur in automatically labeled data? Conduct error analysis on the 500 manually evaluated samples. Categorize errors (e.g., arguments in different contexts, trigger polysemy, missing arguments, incorrect argument roles). Report error distribution. How do these errors impact downstream extraction performance?

How sensitive are results to hyperparameter choices? Provide sensitivity analysis for k (number of key arguments) and TR threshold (0.8). Report performance across range of values for each event type. Analyze whether optimal hyperparameters vary by event type. Provide guidance for selecting hyperparameters for new event types.

Report p-values and 95% confidence intervals. This is critical for validating claims about KR, TR, and FrameNet effectiveness. (2) Validate the Freebase-FrameNet mapping quality by manually evaluating a sample of mappings (50-100) and reporting mapping accuracy. Analyze mapping errors and compare with alternative mapping methods. This is essential for understanding trigger detection reliability. (3) Provide stratified manual evaluation across all 21 event types, with sample size proportional to event type frequency or fixed per event type. Report precision separately for each event type to identify potential biases. (4) Add ablation studies: (a) separate FrameNet filtering vs. expansion effects by reporting results for filtering-only and expansion-only conditions, (b) compare DMCNN with and without MIL on automatically labeled data to quantify MIL contribution. (5) Extend evaluation to more Freebase event types (if possible) and discuss generalization to unmapped types. (6) Provide computational cost analysis (runtime, memory, scalability) to support feasibility claims. (7) Conduct error analysis on manually evaluated samples to characterize error types and validate the soft distant supervision assumption. These revisions will substantially strengthen the paper's methodological rigor and increase confidence in the reported results.
human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
This paper proposes a knowledge-driven methodology for automatically generating large-scale labeled training data for event extraction by combining Freebase (world knowledge) and FrameNet (linguistic knowledge). The core contribution is a soft distant supervision (SDS) framework adapted from relation extraction to event extraction, featuring key argument detection (Key Rate metric), trigger word detection (Trigger Rate metric), FrameNet-based filtering/expansion, and multi-instance learning for noise mitigation. The paper generates 72,611 automatically labeled sentences with reported quality of 88.9% precision for triggers and 85.4% for arguments, and demonstrates utility by improving event extraction performance when combined with human-annotated ACE data (F1: 70.5 vs. 69.1 baseline).

Strengths:
- Well-motivated problem formulation: Clearly articulates limitations of supervised event extraction (expensive annotation, low coverage in ACE 2005) and motivates automatic data labeling as solution.
- Sound methodological approach: Four-stage pipeline is logically coherent and addresses specific challenges at each stage. Soft distant supervision assumption is reasonable.
- Comprehensive evaluation strategy: Multiple complementary evaluation approaches (manual, automatic, held-out, human evaluation) provide multi-faceted validation.
- Substantial practical dataset contribution: 72,611 automatically labeled sentences (12× larger than ACE 2005) released for community use.
- Demonstrated practical utility: Combining automatically labeled data with human-annotated ACE data improves event extraction performance.
- Ablation studies for proposed metrics: Tables 5-6 demonstrate that proposed metrics outperform single-factor baselines.
- Clear presentation: Well-written with effective visual aids and concrete examples.

Limitations:
- Absence of statistical significance testing: No p-values, confidence intervals, or significance tests for any improvements in Tables 4-6. Improvements range from 0.2-5.2 F1 points, but without statistical validation, it is unclear whether differences are meaningful or within noise margins. This is a critical methodological flaw.
- Manual evaluation sample concerns: Only 500 samples from 72,611 (0.69% sample rate) without stratification by event type. Sample may be biased toward high-quality event types. Reported precision figures (88.9%, 85.4%) lack confidence intervals and may overestimate true dataset quality.
- Unvalidated critical assumption: Freebase-FrameNet mapping (Equation 7) uses word embedding similarity but no validation of mapping quality, error analysis, or comparison with alternative methods provided. This directly impacts trigger filtering/expansion effectiveness.
- Incomplete ablation studies: (1) FrameNet filtering vs. expansion effects not decomposed; unclear which operation drives 1.0-1.7 F1 improvement. (2) No direct DMCNN vs. DMCNN-MIL comparison; Figures 7-8 lack numerical values; Table 7 incomplete.
- Limited generalization scope: Only 4 Freebase event types mapped to ACE; only 21 of 1,885 Freebase CVTs evaluated. Generalization to unmapped types and all CVTs unclear.

Open Questions:
- Are the reported improvements statistically significant? What are the 95% confidence intervals for F1 scores in Tables 4-6? Conduct paired t-tests or bootstrap confidence intervals to determine whether improvements are meaningful or within noise margins.
- How representative is the 500-sample manual evaluation? What is the distribution of samples across the 21 event types? Does precision vary significantly across event types? Conduct stratified sampling and report precision separately for each event type.
- What is the quality of Freebase-FrameNet mappings? Manually evaluate a sample of mappings (50-100) to assess accuracy. How do incorrect mappings impact trigger detection and overall performance?
- What are the individual contributions of FrameNet filtering vs. expansion? Provide ablation results for filtering-only, expansion-only, and both to clarify which operation drives the 1.0-1.7 F1 improvement.
- How much does multi-instance learning contribute to noise mitigation? Provide direct comparison of DMCNN with and without MIL on automatically labeled data. Provide numerical values for Figures 7-8.
- How do results generalize to unmapped event types and to all 1,885 Freebase CVTs? Explicitly list the 4 event types mapped from Freebase to ACE. Evaluate on additional event types if possible.
- What types of errors occur in automatically labeled data? Conduct error analysis on the 500 manually evaluated samples. Categorize errors and report error distribution.
- How sensitive are results to hyperparameter choices? Provide sensitivity analysis for k and TR threshold. Provide guidance for selecting hyperparameters for new event types.

Transparency:
The paper exhibits several transparency gaps: (1) Statistical significance testing is absent throughout, preventing assessment of whether improvements are meaningful. (2) Manual evaluation methodology lacks key details (no stratification by event type, event type distribution unknown, no confidence intervals). (3) Freebase-FrameNet mapping validation is absent (no error analysis, no comparison with alternative methods, no specification of word embeddings used). (4) Hyperparameter sensitivity analysis is incomplete (no TR threshold sensitivity, no guidance for new event types). (5) Ablation studies are incomplete (FrameNet filtering vs. expansion not separated, DMCNN vs. DMCNN-MIL comparison missing). (6) Figures 7-8 lack numerical values; Table 7 incomplete. (7) Event type mapping from Freebase to ACE lacks specification of mapping criteria and inter-annotator agreement. (8) Computational cost and scalability claims are not quantified. (9) Reproducibility is compromised by missing details (word embedding method, DMCNN-MIL training procedure, significance testing methodology).

top_documents.abstract_or_snippet: Exploiting Parallel News Streams for Unsupervised Event Extraction Congle Zhang, Stephen Soderland & Daniel S. Weld Computer Science & Engineering University of Washington Seattle, W A 98195, USA {clzhang, soderlan, weld }@cs.washington.edu Abstract Most approaches to relation extraction , the task of extracting ground facts from natural language text, are based on machine learning and thus starved by scarce training data. Man- ual annotation is too expensive to scale to a comprehensive set of relations. Distant super- vision, which automatically creates training data, only works with relations that already populate a knowledge base (KB). Unfortu- nately, KBs such as FreeBase rarely cover event relations ( e.g. “person travels to loca- tion”). Thus, the problem of extracting a wide range of events — e.g., from news streams — is an important, open challenge. This paper introduces N EWS SPIKE -RE, a novel, unsupervised algorithm that discovers event relations and then learns to extract them. NEWS SPIKE -RE uses a novel probabilistic graphical model to cluster sentences describ- ing similar events from parallel news streams. These clusters then comprise training data for the extractor. Our evaluation shows that NEWS SPIKE -RE generates high quality train- ing sentences and learns extractors that per- form much better than rival approaches, more than doubling the area under a precision-recall curve compared to Universal Schemas. 1

Weld Computer Science & Engineering University of Washington Seattle, W A 98195, USA {clzhang, soderlan, weld }@cs.washington.edu Abstract Most approaches to relation extraction , the task of extracting ground facts from natural language text, are based on machine learning and thus starved by scarce training data. Man- ual annotation is too expensive to scale to a comprehensive set of relations. Distant super- vision, which automatically creates training data, only works with relations that already populate a knowledge base (KB). Unfortu- nately, KBs such as FreeBase rarely cover event relations ( e.g. “person travels to loca- tion”). Thus, the problem of extracting a wide range of events — e.g., from news streams — is an important, open challenge. This paper introduces N EWS SPIKE -RE, a novel, unsupervised algorithm that discovers event relations and then learns to extract them. NEWS SPIKE -RE uses a novel probabilistic graphical model to cluster sentences describ- ing similar events from parallel news streams. These clusters then comprise training data for the extractor. Our evaluation shows that NEWS SPIKE -RE generates high quality train- ing sentences and learns extractors that per- form much better than rival approaches, more than doubling the area under a precision-recall curve compared to Universal Schemas. 1

These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 5. Check that your scores reflect the review I3
Codes: I3
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: Starting with February 2025, ARR reviewers are asked to provide three scores: soundness, excitement, and overall recommendation. I3 The soundness scores must be justified by the text of the review . If you give a low Soundness score without finding any major faults, this means that your review is not a faithful explanation of your recommendation, and you need to revise it. One possible reason for low soundness scores without sufficient justification could be reliance on some unconscious bias or heuristic, like the ones listed in the previous section. Likewise, low reproducibility scores should be justified. Sometimes you may find the work sound, but not something that is interesting for you personally. Such preferences are more subjective and should be reflected in a separate excitement score, which is orthogonal to the assessment of the soundness of the paper. Excitement scores reflect our personal taste, and so do not necessarily come with explicit reasons. The Overall assessment score is an explicit recommendation for the outcome of this paper, if it were committed to an *ACL venue. This is a composite score reflecting your assessment of soundness, excitement, and also other factors like novelty and impact. All papers recommended for Findings and main conferences are expected to be sufficiently sound and reproducible, but you may consider a paper worthy of the main conference even if you personally are not excited about it.

Weld Computer Science & Engineering University of Washington Seattle, W A 98195, USA {clzhang, soderlan, weld }@cs.washington.edu Abstract Most approaches to relation extraction , the task of extracting ground facts from natural language text, are based on machine learning and thus starved by scarce training data. Man- ual annotation is too expensive to scale to a comprehensive set of relations. Distant super- vision, which automatically creates training data, only works with relations that already populate a knowledge base (KB). Unfortu- nately, KBs such as FreeBase rarely cover event relations ( e.g. “person travels to loca- tion”). Thus, the problem of extracting a wide range of events — e.g., from news streams — is an important, open challenge. This paper introduces N EWS SPIKE -RE, a novel, unsupervised algorithm that discovers event relations and then learns to extract them. NEWS SPIKE -RE uses a novel probabilistic graphical model to cluster sentences describ- ing similar events from parallel news streams. These clusters then comprise training data for the extractor. Our evaluation shows that NEWS SPIKE -RE generates high quality train- ing sentences and learns extractors that per- form much better than rival approaches, more than doubling the area under a precision-recall curve compared to Universal Schemas. 1

Section: Q: Why is peer review so inconsistent?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: much attention. In case of submissions that get deanonymized due to preprints and social media, we may also be biased in favor of well-known authors and/or widely-discussed papers. These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.

Content: much attention. In case of submissions that get deanonymized due to preprints and social media, we may also be biased in favor of well-known authors and/or widely-discussed papers. These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.

Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. Weld Computer Science & Engineering University of Washington Seattle, W A 98195, USA {clzhang, soderlan, weld }@cs.washington.edu Abstract Most approaches to relation extraction , the task of extracting ground facts from natural language text, are based on machine learning and thus starved by scarce training data. Man- ual annotation is too expensive to scale to a comprehensive set of relations. Distant super- vision, which automatically creates training data, only works with relations that already populate a knowledge base (KB). Unfortu- nately, KBs such as FreeBase rarely cover event relations ( e.g. “person travels to loca- tion”). Thus, the problem of extracting a wide range of events — e.g., from news streams — is an important, open challenge. This paper introduces N EWS SPIKE -RE, a novel, unsupervised algorithm that discovers event relations and then learns to extract them. NEWS SPIKE -RE uses a novel probabilistic graphical model to cluster sentences describ- ing similar events from parallel news streams. These clusters then comprise training data for the extractor.
